lessons.title: Correlated Subqueries
lessons.concept: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and is evaluated once per row (conceptually) of the outer query. It is useful for row-by-row comparisons such as finding rows greater than their group's average or employees earning more than their department average.
lessons.formula: Example: SELECT e1.* FROM emp e1 WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept); inner query depends on e1.
lessons.worked_example: For each employee row, compute average salary of that employee's department and compare; correlated because inner query uses e1.dept from outer row.
mistakes: Assuming correlated subqueries run only once like non-correlated ones
Missing correlation condition causing incorrect results or full rescans
Performance issues on large data without proper indexing
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: EXISTS, IN, and ANY/ALL
lessons.concept: EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any rows (often efficient with correlation). IN compares a value to a list/set from subquery. ANY/SOME and ALL compare a value to each value returned (e.g., > ANY means greater than at least one; > ALL means greater than every value).
lessons.formula: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE correlated). WHERE x IN (subquery). WHERE x > ANY (subquery). WHERE x > ALL (subquery).
lessons.worked_example: Customers who placed orders: SELECT * FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id=c.id). Salary > ALL (subquery of manager salaries) means higher than every manager salary (i.e., higher than max).
mistakes: NULL handling differences with NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS in some cases
Using IN with subqueries returning unintended duplicates/NULLs without care
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Subqueries in FROM and SELECT (Derived/Scalar)
lessons.concept: Subqueries in FROM act as derived tables (inline views) and must usually have an alias. Scalar subqueries in SELECT return a single value per outer row (or NULL) and can compute related aggregates. These forms help structure complex queries.
lessons.formula: SELECT a, (SELECT MAX(b) FROM t2 WHERE t2.id=t1.id) AS mx FROM t1; SELECT * FROM (SELECT dept, AVG(sal) av FROM emp GROUP BY dept) d WHERE d.av > 50000;
lessons.worked_example: Derived table computes department averages, outer query filters departments above threshold. Scalar subquery can attach a per-row computed value.
mistakes: Forgetting alias for derived table in FROM (required in many DBMSs)
Scalar subquery returning more than one row causing error
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.
